title: Electrolysis of aqueous solutions
aim: To investigate what is formed at each electrode when different aqueous solutions are electrolysed using inert electrodes, and to identify any gases produced.
background: Electrolysis uses a direct current (d.c.) to break down an ionic compound that is molten or dissolved in water (the electrolyte). Positive ions move to the negative electrode (cathode) and negative ions move to the positive electrode (anode). Inert electrodes, such as graphite (carbon), conduct electricity but do not react themselves.

In an aqueous solution, water also provides ions: some water molecules ionise to form hydrogen ions (H⁺) and hydroxide ions (OH⁻). So there are two possible positive ions and two possible negative ions, and only one of each is discharged.

At the cathode: if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen (for example sodium or potassium), hydrogen gas is produced. If the metal is less reactive than hydrogen (for example copper or silver), the metal is deposited.

At the anode: if the solution contains halide ions (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻), the halogen is produced (chlorine, bromine or iodine). If there are no halide ions, for example in sulfate or nitrate solutions, oxygen is produced from hydroxide ions.
Gases are identified with tests: hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop with a lighted splint, oxygen relights a glowing splint, and chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper white.
hypothesis: Copper will be deposited at the cathode from solutions of copper salts, but hydrogen will be produced from sodium salts because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen. Chlorine will be produced at the anode from chloride solutions and oxygen from sulfate solutions.

variables.independent: The solution being electrolysed (copper(II) chloride, sodium chloride, copper(II) sulfate, sodium sulfate).
variables.dependent: The product formed at each electrode (identified by observations and gas tests).
control: Voltage of the d.c. supply (4 V)
Time the current flows before testing (about 5 minutes)

equipment: Electrolysis cell: a small plastic container with two graphite rod electrodes fixed through a rubber bung in its base
Two graphite rod electrodes (fitted in the cell)
Low-voltage d.c. power supply (set to 4 V)
Two crocodile clips and connecting leads
Two small test tubes (to collect gases)
Solutions (0.5 mol/dm³): copper(II) chloride, sodium chloride, copper(II) sulfate, sodium sulfate
Blue litmus paper and distilled water
Wooden splints and a Bunsen burner or lighter
method: Pour about 50 cm³ of copper(II) chloride solution into the electrolysis cell so that both graphite electrodes are well covered. Check that the electrodes do not touch each other.

Fill two small test tubes completely with the same solution. Put your thumb over the end, turn each one upside down under the surface of the solution, and place it over an electrode so that any gas given off collects in the tube.

Use leads (and crocodile clips if needed) to connect the electrodes to a low-voltage d.c. power supply. Label which electrode is connected to the negative terminal (cathode) and which to the positive terminal (anode).
Use crocodile clips and leads to connect the rods to the d.c. power supply. Label which rod is connected to the negative terminal (cathode) and which to the positive terminal (anode).
Turn on the power supply at 4 V. Watch both electrodes and record what you see (bubbles, a coating, a colour change).
Hold a piece of damp blue litmus paper near the top of the anode using forceps. If it turns red and then white (is bleached), chlorine is being produced.

When a test tube is about half full of gas, test it. For a gas at the cathode, put a lighted splint near the mouth: a squeaky pop shows hydrogen. For a gas at the anode that does not bleach litmus, put in a glowing splint: if it relights, the gas is oxygen.
Turn off the power supply after about 5 minutes. Pour away the solution into a waste container and look at the cathode for any coating of metal (copper is pink-brown).
Clean the electrodes (or use new ones) and repeat the experiment with sodium chloride solution, copper(II) sulfate solution and sodium sulfate solution.
Record the product at each electrode for every solution in a results table.

safety.hazard: Chlorine gas produced at the anode
safety.risk: Toxic; irritates the lungs and eyes, especially for people with asthma.
safety.precaution: Run the electrolysis for only a few minutes, keep the room well ventilated (or use a fume cupboard), and turn off the power as soon as the test is done.

safety.hazard: Copper(II) chloride and copper(II) sulfate solutions
safety.risk: Harmful if swallowed and irritant to eyes and skin; toxic to aquatic life.
safety.precaution: Wear eye protection, avoid skin contact, wash hands, and pour waste copper solutions into a labelled waste container.

safety.hazard: Hydrogen gas tested with a lighted splint
safety.risk: Small explosion (pop) and burns from the splint.
safety.precaution: Only test small volumes in a test tube and keep flames away from the solutions and from other people.

safety.risk: Electric shock or short circuit if the electrodes touch.
safety.precaution: Use a low-voltage supply (no more than 6 V), keep the electrodes apart, and turn the power off before handling the electrodes.

results.notes: Use the reactivity series to explain the cathode product and the presence or absence of halide ions to explain the anode product. For sodium sulfate, the volume of hydrogen collected is about twice the volume of oxygen because water is being split into H₂ and O₂ in a 2 : 1 ratio.

analysis: Copper was deposited at the cathode from both copper solutions because copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so Cu²⁺ ions are discharged in preference to H⁺ ions: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.
Hydrogen was produced at the cathode from both sodium solutions because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions (from water) are discharged instead of Na⁺ ions: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
Chlorine was produced at the anode from both chloride solutions because halide ions are discharged in preference to hydroxide ions: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
Oxygen was produced at the anode from both sulfate solutions because sulfate ions are not discharged; hydroxide ions from water are discharged instead: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻.

Reduction (gain of electrons) happens at the cathode and oxidation (loss of electrons) happens at the anode. After electrolysis of sodium chloride solution, the sodium ions and hydroxide ions left behind form sodium hydroxide solution.

errors.error: Some chlorine dissolves in the water, so less gas collects than expected and the litmus test may be slow.
errors.improvement: Hold damp litmus paper directly above the anode as soon as bubbles appear, rather than relying on the volume collected.

errors.error: Not enough gas is collected to test it reliably.
errors.improvement: Run the electrolysis for longer, or use a slightly higher voltage (still low voltage), before testing the gas.

errors.error: Copper from a previous experiment left on the electrode could be mistaken for a new deposit.
errors.improvement: Clean the electrodes with emery paper between experiments, or use fresh electrodes.

errors.error: Electrodes touching each other cause a short circuit and no electrolysis.
errors.improvement: Use a cell with the rods fixed firmly through the base (or a lid) so they stay a fixed distance apart.

examTips: Learn the two rules. Cathode: metal if less reactive than hydrogen, otherwise hydrogen. Anode: halogen if a halide is present, otherwise oxygen.
Remember PANIC: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode. Positive ions (cations) go to the cathode; negative ions (anions) go to the anode.
Learn the gas tests exactly: hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint; oxygen relights a glowing splint; chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper.
Higher: write half equations with electrons. Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu or 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. Anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ or 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻.
Say 'inert electrodes (graphite)' and explain they do not react with the products, so they do not affect the result.

markScheme: 1 mark: copper
questions.explanation: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper ions are discharged at the cathode as a pink-brown coating. Oxygen forms at the anode, not the cathode.

questions.question: Describe the test for chlorine gas and give the positive result.
markScheme: 1 mark: hold damp (blue) litmus paper in the gas
1 mark: the litmus paper is bleached / turns white
questions.explanation: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper. Blue litmus may turn red first because chlorine forms an acidic solution, then turns white. The paper must be damp.

questions.question:
Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes.
Which row, A, B, C or D, in Table 1 shows the products?
markScheme: 1 mark: cathode hydrogen and anode chlorine
questions.explanation: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen is produced at the cathode. Chloride ions are present, so chlorine is produced at the anode. Sodium is only produced when molten sodium chloride is electrolysed.

questions.question: Explain why hydrogen, not sodium, is produced at the cathode when sodium sulfate solution is electrolysed.
acceptedAnswers: sodium is more reactive than hydrogen
markScheme: 1 mark: sodium is more reactive than hydrogen
1 mark: so hydrogen ions (from water) are discharged / gain electrons instead of sodium ions
questions.explanation: Water provides H⁺ ions. At the cathode, the ion of the less reactive element is discharged, and hydrogen is less reactive than sodium.

questions.question: Which gas is produced at the anode when copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes?
markScheme: 1 mark: oxygen
questions.explanation: There are no halide ions in copper sulfate solution, so hydroxide ions from water are discharged to form oxygen. Sulfate ions are not discharged.

questions.question:
A student electrolysed a solution using graphite electrodes.
Table 1 shows the result of a test on the gas collected at the anode.
Name the gas and suggest a solution that could have been electrolysed to produce it.

rows: Glowing splint placed in the gas

markScheme: 1 mark: oxygen
1 mark: any solution without halide ions, for example copper(II) sulfate, sodium sulfate, or a nitrate solution
questions.explanation: Oxygen relights a glowing splint. It forms at the anode when the solution has no chloride, bromide or iodide ions.

questions.question: Explain why graphite is used for the electrodes in this practical.
markScheme: 1 mark: graphite is inert / unreactive so it does not react with the electrolyte or products (and it conducts electricity)
questions.explanation: Inert electrodes take no part in the reaction, so the products depend only on the ions in the solution. A reactive electrode, such as copper, would itself dissolve at the anode.

questions.question:
A student electrolysed copper(II) chloride solution using graphite electrodes.
The student measured the mass of the cathode before and after the electrolysis.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mass of copper deposited on the cathode.
questions.explanation: The increase in mass of the cathode is the mass of copper deposited on it.

questions.question:
A student electrolysed sodium sulfate solution and collected the gases produced at each electrode.
Table 1 shows the results.
The overall reaction is:
2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)
Calculate volume V, the volume of oxygen expected at the anode in the same time.

headers: Volume of gas collected in cm³

markScheme: 1 mark: ratio H₂ : O₂ = 2 : 1
questions.explanation: Equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules at the same temperature and pressure, so the volume ratio is the mole ratio, 2 : 1. In practice slightly less oxygen is collected because some dissolves.

questions.question: Which half equation shows the reaction at the anode when sodium sulfate solution is electrolysed?
markScheme: 1 mark: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻
questions.explanation: Hydroxide ions lose electrons (are oxidised) at the anode to form oxygen and water. 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ happens at the cathode. Sulfate ions are not discharged.

questions.question: Write the half equation for the reaction at the cathode when copper(II) chloride solution is electrolysed, and state whether this is oxidation or reduction.
markScheme: 1 mark: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu
1 mark: reduction, because the copper ions gain electrons
questions.explanation: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain of electrons. Positive ions gain electrons at the cathode, so reduction always occurs at the cathode.

questions.question: Potassium bromide solution is electrolysed with graphite electrodes. Which observation would be made at the anode?
options: Colourless bubbles that relight a glowing splint
The solution around the electrode turns orange-brown
Colourless bubbles that burn with a squeaky pop
markScheme: 1 mark: solution turns orange-brown (bromine is formed)
questions.explanation: Bromide ions are halide ions, so bromine forms at the anode and dissolves to give an orange-brown solution. Hydrogen, not potassium, forms at the cathode.

questions.question:
A student electrolyses copper(II) chloride solution.
Give one safety precaution the student should take, and explain why it is needed. Give a second safety precaution.
markScheme: 1 mark: any one precaution: work in a well-ventilated room or fume cupboard; run for only a short time; wear eye protection; use a low-voltage supply
1 mark: matching explanation, for example because chlorine is a toxic gas / copper chloride is harmful and irritant
questions.explanation: The main hazard is the toxic chlorine produced at the anode, so it should not be allowed to build up in the room.

questions.question:
Describe how a student could electrolyse sodium chloride solution and identify the products at both electrodes.
Include the expected results and an explanation of them.
markScheme: Indicative content: pour sodium chloride solution into an electrolysis cell or beaker; use two inert graphite electrodes held apart (fixed through the base or a lid); connect to a low-voltage d.c. supply; invert test tubes full of solution over each electrode to collect gases; switch on and observe bubbles at both electrodes; test gas at the cathode with a lighted splint: squeaky pop shows hydrogen; hold damp litmus near the anode: bleached shows chlorine; hydrogen forms because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen so H⁺ ions from water are discharged; chlorine forms because chloride (halide) ions are discharged at the anode; carry out in a well-ventilated room because chlorine is toxic
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent method with correct apparatus and gas collection, both correct gas tests and results, and explanations of both products using reactivity and halide ions.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a workable method with at least one correct test and product, and some explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, such as pass electricity through salt water and test the gases, with little detail.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The question asks for method, results and explanation. Many students describe the apparatus but forget to explain why hydrogen (not sodium) forms at the cathode.
